newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian govt supports health insurance reform.
newsitem.headline: Australian govt supports health insurance reform.

text.p: CANBERRA, April 10 - The Australian government on Thursday supported reforms to private health insurance, but said it would maintain a system banning different premiums for different customers.

Health Minister Michael Wooldridge endorsed some key proposals by the government's Productivity Commission, including penalties for people who delay taking out health cover until later in life, allowance of hostile takeovers of insurance companies and an end to monitoring of premiums.

"Together with the private health insurance incentives which are available from July 1, the reforms I have announced today will make health insurance fairer, more affordable, more customer-friendly and better value," Wooldridge said in a statement.

The Liberal-National government announced in its 1996/97 budget tax incentives worth about A$500 million a year to encourage people to take out private health insurance and wean higher income people off the public Medicare health system.
Wooldrige said on Thursday government support for penalties for people joining funds late in life needed further analysis.

"It has been evident for some years that the industry needs a circuit breaker to allow funds to stabilise their cost base, make it more affordable for members and develop better, cheaper and more innovative forms of health cover to attract younger, healthier people," he said.
"We are helping people meet the costs of their health cover, and giving the funds the freedom they need to get their costs under control and get better products into the market."
The government also said it supported in principle an end to monitoring of premiums, subject to talks with the industry on voluntary guidelines, he said.
